rv.q: Mark Strong’s politician kicks back with his wife (Lesley Manville), his family and his campaign team, confident that his message of change and hope has won the day. But this is Robert Icke’s stunning reworking of Oedipus. As that digital clock in the campaign room counts down remorselessly, we watch in queasy horror.

It is not only about a couple doomed by their love but contains cross currents of family drama, from mother-daughter battles to a son’s coming out and profound reflections on life, death and sex. A stop-clock counts the hours and minutes to the election results but also marks the inevitable forward movement to terrible self-knowledge.
Mark Strong and Lesley Manville are spellbinding in this wrenchingly tense Greek tragedy

The piece has a cumulative power that builds gradually until the atmosphere is riveting
Robert Icke’s compassionate political thriller spin on the horrifying Greek tragedy

Icke is usually excellent at sustaining tension through the electric space he generates between his actors; here, that space feels slack. The dialogue is sometimes flabby; there is an unnecessary intrusive coda.
Any opportunity to see Mark Strong — who takes the title role previously played by Hans Kesting — has to be seized with both hands.

The voting has just closed and cameras are following this would-be ruler’s progress to power. To anyone who already knows that Oedipus’s evening will end with him being unable to see anybody or anything, it’s one of a slew of smart ironies in Robert Icke’s riveting modern-day rejig.

The Oscar-winning star is the uncanny centre of this season’s second take on the tragedy Oedipus, following Robert Icke’s brilliantly imagined modern-day political retelling last year. It could be classical overkill.
The adaptation excels in the way that Icke identifies the tragedy as being not of one man
